processing: As with other Dancong: withered, repeatedly tossed for partial oxidation, fixed, rolled and dried over heat. Little is published about any method specific to this strain.
harvest_season: Usually spring, as with most prized Dancong; picking from the old named trees is very limited.
appearance_dry: Typically long, straight, dark brown strips with an oily sheen, as is usual for the gardenia-aroma Dancong group.
appearance_liquor: Bright orange-yellow, as is typical of the gardenia-aroma group.
appearance_wet: Typically thick leaves with reddened edges, as with other tossed Dancong.
taste_profile: Belongs to the gardenia aroma group, so expect a high gardenia note, a full fresh body and a persistent sweet return, as is typical of that group.

brewing.notes: Keep steeps short, as with any Dancong: the leaf turns bitter quickly when left in the water.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest, usually spring of the current year or a year or two later after further roasting. Leaf from a truly old Song Zhong tree is scarce, while plenty of tea carries the name with only cuttings or marketing behind it, so ask which tree or strain is meant.
description:
Song Cha is the short trade name for Song Zhong, the old strain from Wudong in the Fenghuang mountains of Guangdong that is usually grouped with gardenia-aroma Dancong. It should not be confused with the Song dynasty's whisked teas, which share the Chinese words and nothing else.

The making is that of Dancong in general: withering, long rounds of tossing that bruise the leaf edges, then fixing, rolling and drying. Nothing specific to this strain is well documented, so expect the method to vary by maker.

In the cup, expect what the gardenia group is known for: a high floral aroma, a full and fresh body and a sweet return that lasts. Use a small gaiwan, plenty of leaf and very short steeps.

The word Song is the thing to question when buying. Reported tree ages differ widely from one account to another, so treat a seller's story with care and let the price and the cup decide.
history:
The strain has gone through many names. One Chinese account lists Tuan Shu Ye, Da Ye Xiang, Yan Shang Zhen, Huang Zhi Xiang and Feng Chan Cha, then Dong Fang Hong from 1969, with Song Zhong Dancong restored in 1980 and shortened in the trade to Song Cha.

A legend says the last Song emperor, Zhao Bing, fleeing south and thirsty, was served tea here and gave it the name. It is only a legend. The age of the old trees is also unsettled: Chinese reports give figures from about 400 years to over 700 for different trees, and one of the oldest, known as Song Zhong No. 1, is reported to have died in 2016.
